Shalt
shalt
v. (second person singular of shall; rendering Hebrew imperfect of command, Greek future indicative)
From Saxon scealt, second person singular of sceal, to owe or be obliged. The root sense is obligation, not mere futurity — a fact that governs its use in the law. Thou shalt is not a prediction about the future; it is a bond laid on the person addressed.

Biblical Definition

Shalt is the second person singular of shall, and it is the verb of the commandment. The Decalogue is built of it: “Thou shalt have no other gods before me”, “Thou shalt not kill”, and eight more, every one singular and every one binding a particular Israelite rather than the nation collectively. The old English sense of obligation is the reason the translators chose it, and it is why the commandments read as debts owed rather than events foreseen. But the same word also carries the warning — “in the day that thou eatest thereof thou shalt surely die” — and the promise, as when Job is told, “the Almighty shall be thy defence, and thou shalt have plenty of silver” (Job 22:25). It governs the sabbath of the land: “thou shalt neither sow thy field, nor prune thy vineyard” (Leviticus 25:4), a command that required Israel to trust God's provision for a year at a time. Obligation, threat, and promise all run through this one form, which is fitting, since in Scripture they are never far apart.

Webster 1828 Definition

The second person singular of shall; used only with thou. Its root sense is obligation rather than futurity, which is why it is the verb of the Decalogue — thou shalt and thou shalt not bind the person addressed rather than predicting what he will do.

expand to see more

SHALT, v. [Sax. scealt.] The second person singular of shall; as, thou shalt.

2. The primary sense of shall is to owe, to be under obligation; hence its use in commands and laws.

3. In the second and third persons it expresses promise, command, determination or threatening.

4. It is used only with thou; with ye or you the form is shall.

5. In Scripture, Thou shalt have no other gods before me, Exo. 20; Thou shalt not kill, Exo. 20.

Key Scripture

Exodus 20:3 — "Thou shalt have no other gods before me."

Exodus 20:13 — "Thou shalt not kill."

Leviticus 25:4 — "But in the seventh year shall be a sabbath of rest unto the land, a sabbath for the LORD: thou shalt neither sow thy field, nor prune thy vineyard."

Job 22:25 — "Yea, the Almighty shall be thy defence, and thou shalt have plenty of silver."

Modern Corruption

The commandments are widely reduced to advice, ideals, or descriptions of a flourishing life — suggestions a man may weigh. The verb forbids that reading: shalt is the language of obligation imposed by a Lawgiver, and its force does not depend on the hearer's agreement.

expand to see more

Two opposite errors flatten the imperative. The first empties the law of authority by recasting it as wisdom for human flourishing — the commandments become sound advice, useful because they work, and therefore negotiable when they appear not to. The second empties it by antinomianism, treating the moral law as wholly abolished for the believer so that thou shalt not no longer addresses him at all. The 1689 Confession answers both: the moral law forever binds all, justified persons as well as others, though believers are not under it as a covenant of works for justification.

The right use of the imperative is the one the Reformed tradition has always taught. The law shows the sinner his guilt and drives him to Christ; it restrains evil in society; and it directs the believer's obedience out of gratitude, not for acceptance. Christ Himself intensified rather than relaxed it, moving each thou shalt not inward to the heart. To recover the weight of the word is not legalism, which is the attempt to be justified by keeping it; it is simply hearing the Lawgiver speak in the mood He actually used.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew commands by the imperative or by the imperfect with the negative lo', which is the absolute prohibition of the Decalogue; Greek renders these by the future indicative, which is why the New Testament citations read thou shalt not.

expand to see more

Hebrew lo' (H3808) — not; with the imperfect it forms the absolute, permanent prohibition of the Ten Commandments.

Hebrew imperfect of command — a form expressing binding obligation rather than simple future time.

Greek future indicative — the form used in the Septuagint and the New Testament to render the Hebrew prohibitions.

Saxon sceal — to owe, to be obliged; the root sense that made shall the proper verb for law.

Hebrew mitzvah (H4687) — a commandment; that which is laid upon a man by authority.

Usage

"Of the first commandment binding each Israelite singly: Thou shalt have no other gods before me (Exodus 20:3)."

"Of the sixth commandment in its briefest form: Thou shalt not kill (Exodus 20:13)."

"Of the sabbath required of the land itself: thou shalt neither sow thy field, nor prune thy vineyard (Leviticus 25:4)."
